questions.title: How can a court grant a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal based on the affirmative defense of fair use at the pleading stage?
questions.question_body: I understand that fair use is typically an affirmative defense that requires fact-intensive discovery and is usually reserved for summary judgment or trial. However, in *Santos v. Kimmel*, the Second Circuit affirmed the dismissal of the copyright claims under Rule 12(b)(6), stating the defense was 'so clearly established by the complaint.' What is the procedural standard for deciding fair use on a motion to dismiss? Does the plaintiff essentially have to plead themselves out of court by admitting facts that make fair use undeniable?

questions.title: Why did the court reject Santos's argument that Kimmel's deception regarding his identity negated the 'transformative' nature of the use?
questions.question_body: Santos argued that because Kimmel lied to get the videos made, he couldn't claim the use was transformative (commentary vs. personal message). The court relied on *Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith* to say subjective intent doesn't matter, focusing instead on what a 'reasonable observer' perceives. How does this objective 'reasonable observer' test work when the context of creation involves fraud? If the creator didn't know they were being mocked, how can the resulting work be considered a commentary on their willingness to be mocked?

questions.title: Does the 'bad faith' requirement from *Harper & Row* still survive as a barrier to fair use after recent Supreme Court precedent?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions *Harper & Row*'s statement that 'fair use presupposes good faith,' but then immediately says the Supreme Court has 'distanced itself' from this. Given that Kimmel actively deceived Santos to procure the footage, why wasn't this considered bad faith sufficient to kill the fair use defense? Is 'bad faith' now irrelevant in Second Circuit fair use analysis unless it directly relates to market substitution?

questions.title: How does the court distinguish between market harm caused by criticism versus market harm caused by substitution in Factor Four?
questions.question_body: Regarding the fourth fair use factor, Santos seemed to argue that airing these videos damaged his brand and future earning potential. The court rejected this, citing *Campbell* and *Hachette*, saying we don't care if criticism devalues the work, only if it acts as a substitute. Can someone explain the line between 'devaluing through parody' (which is allowed) and 'usurping the market'? If no one hires Santos anymore because of this segment, isn't that effectively destroying his market for personalized videos?

questions.title: Why did Santos lack standing to sue for breach of contract under the Cameo Terms of Service if he was the content creator?
questions.question_body: The court dismissed the breach of contract claim because Santos wasn't a party to the Terms of Service agreement between Kimmel (the user) and Cameo. This seems counterintuitive since Santos provided the service. Under Illinois law, why is there such a 'strong presumption against conferring benefits to noncontracting third parties' here? Since other parts of the ToS explicitly mentioned third-party beneficiaries, does that imply that where it is silent, creators like Santos intentionally waived their right to enforce user obligations?

questions.title: What specific elements prevented an 'implied-in-fact' contract from existing between Santos and Kimmel despite the transaction occurring?
questions.question_body: Even if there was no written contract between Santos and Kimmel directly, why didn't the act of requesting and paying for a video create an implied-in-fact contract under New York law? The court said Santos failed to allege a 'meeting of minds' regarding specific terms. Isn't there an implicit understanding in every Cameo transaction that the buyer won't misuse the video? What specific factual allegations was Santos missing in his complaint to prove this implied agreement?

questions.title: Why is 'out-of-pocket loss' a mandatory element for fraudulent inducement in New York, and how does it differ from other damages?
questions.question_body: The fraudulent inducement claim was dismissed because Santos didn't allege 'out-of-pocket loss.' He got paid for every video he made, so he didn't lose money on the transactions themselves. But shouldn't reputational damage or lost future earnings count as damages for fraud? Why does New York law strictly require direct financial loss (money spent or lost in the deal) rather than consequential damages for this specific tort?
